notes.b: Your body replaces and repairs tissue by mitosis (cell division that makes two identical cells), and it keeps this tightly controlled. Cancer is what happens when that control fails.
points: Cancer is a group of diseases in which some body cells lose control of mitosis. They divide too often (the rate of division is abnormal) and too many times (the number of divisions is not limited).
Cancer cells can also invade nearby tissues and spread to other parts of the body, which is what makes cancer more than just extra cells.
There are over 200 kinds of cancer, named after the organ or tissue where they start, e.g. lung, breast, skin, bowel and blood.
Carcinomas are the group that start in epithelial tissues (the tissues that line or cover organs), e.g. most lung, breast and bowel cancers.
Sarcomas start in bone, muscle or connective tissue (the supporting tissue that holds other tissues together).
Leukaemias start in the blood-forming cells of the bone marrow, and lymphomas start in the lymphatic system (the network of vessels and nodes that drains fluid and carries immune cells).
Cancer starts from a single cell whose DNA has changed (mutated). All the cancer cells in a tumour are descended from that one cell by mitosis, so they all carry its mutation.
notes.tip: A common exam question is simply what cancer is. Say that cells lose control of both the rate and the number of divisions, and add that they can invade and spread. Fast division alone is not enough for the marks.

notes.h: How normal cell division is regulated
notes.b: To see how cancer starts, you first need to know how healthy cells stay in check. Normal cells divide only when told to, and have built-in ways to stop damaged cells from dividing.
points: Normal cells divide only when they receive signals to divide (growth factors, chemical messengers from other cells), and stop when signals tell them to stop.
Checkpoints in the cell cycle (the ordered series of stages a cell goes through to divide) halt the cycle if the DNA is damaged or not copied correctly, so errors are not passed on.
Two groups of genes control this. Proto-oncogenes code for proteins that stimulate the cell cycle, so they are the accelerator, e.g. growth factor receptors (proteins that detect the growth signal).
Tumour suppressor genes code for proteins that stop the cycle at checkpoints, so they are the brakes. They also repair damaged DNA or make a badly damaged cell destroy itself.
Apoptosis is programmed cell death: a damaged or unwanted cell breaks itself down in a controlled way, without harming neighbouring cells. It removes cells with damaged DNA before they can divide.

TP53 is an example of a tumour suppressor gene. It codes for the protein p53, which stops the cell cycle when DNA is damaged so that the DNA can be repaired, or triggers apoptosis if the damage is too great.
p53 is called the guardian of the genome because it protects the DNA. TP53 is mutated in about half of all human cancers, which shows how important its protection is.
Contact inhibition: normal cells in a tissue, and in a culture dish, stop dividing when they touch neighbouring cells, so they form a single layer.
Most normal human cells can divide only a limited number of times before they stop, because the protective caps at the ends of their chromosomes (telomeres) shorten with each division.
notes.tip: Remember the pairing: proto-oncogenes are the accelerator and tumour suppressor genes are the brakes. Proto-oncogenes are normal, necessary genes, so don't say people have oncogenes just because they have proto-oncogenes.

notes.b: Cancer develops when the genes that control division are damaged by mutation (a change in the DNA). The damage affects the accelerator, the brakes, or both, and it builds up step by step.
points: 1. A mutation in a proto-oncogene can turn it into an oncogene, which is permanently switched on and keeps telling the cell to divide even with no signal, like an accelerator stuck down.
2. A mutation that inactivates a tumour suppressor gene removes the brakes: damaged cells keep dividing instead of stopping, being repaired or dying by apoptosis.
Usually both copies (alleles) of a tumour suppressor gene must be inactivated before control is lost, because one working copy can still make enough of the protein.
3. One mutation is usually not enough. Several mutations in different control genes must build up in the same cell, often over many years.
This is why the risk of most cancers rises with age, and why anything that increases the rate of mutation raises the risk.

4. Once one cell has lost control, every daughter cell inherits the same mutations. As they divide faster and faster, further mutations arise, and the cells that divide fastest or survive best take over, so the cancer cells become more abnormal over time.
5. The immune system (the body's defence against disease) destroys many abnormal cells before they form a tumour. People whose immune system is weakened have a higher risk of some cancers.
notes.tip: A mutated oncogene is a gain of function (a stuck accelerator), while a mutated tumour suppressor gene is a loss of function (a failed brake). Examiners ask about the roles of both, so don't swap them.

notes.b: Cancer cells differ from normal cells in many ways. Most of the differences come straight from the lost controls on division, and they are best learned as pairs.
points: Division: normal cells divide only when signalled, at a controlled rate. Cancer cells divide rapidly and continuously without signals, and ignore signals to stop.

Lifespan: normal cells divide a limited number of times and die by apoptosis when damaged. Cancer cells avoid apoptosis, and many keep their telomeres long by using the enzyme telomerase, so they can divide indefinitely (immortal cells).
Contact inhibition is lost: cancer cells ignore contact with neighbours and pile up into a mass, whereas normal cells stop at contact.
Specialisation: normal cells are specialised (differentiated) for a job. Cancer cells are unspecialised (poorly differentiated), so they don't carry out the tissue's function.

Appearance under the microscope: cancer cells vary in size and shape and have large, irregular, darkly staining nuclei, often with abnormal numbers of chromosomes, and many are seen dividing. This is how cancer is diagnosed from a biopsy (tissue sample) or smear.
Blood supply: cancer cells can release signals that make new blood vessels grow into the tumour (angiogenesis), supplying the oxygen and nutrients needed for further growth.
Attachment: normal cells stick to their neighbours and stay in place. Cancer cells can lose this adhesion (stickiness), break away and move.

HeLa cells are a famous example of immortal cancer cells. They were taken in 1951 from a cervical cancer of Henrietta Lacks at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore, USA, without her knowledge or consent.

They were the first human cells to keep dividing indefinitely in the laboratory, and they are still used in research worldwide, including in developing the polio vaccine. Her case is a well-known example of the ethics of consent in research.
notes.tip: Answer comparison questions with paired points: say what normal cells do and what cancer cells do for each feature, rather than listing cancer features alone.

notes.b: Not every lump of abnormal cells is cancer. What decides it is whether the cells stay put or invade and spread.
points: A tumour is an abnormal mass of cells produced by uncontrolled division.
A benign tumour grows slowly, is usually enclosed in a capsule (a layer of tissue around it), does not invade surrounding tissue or spread, and its cells look fairly normal.

A benign tumour is usually removable by surgery and not life-threatening, though it can be dangerous if it presses on a vital organ such as the brain. Examples are most moles and warts. A benign tumour is not cancer.
A malignant tumour, which is a cancer, grows quickly, has no capsule, invades and destroys surrounding tissue, can spread around the body, and has abnormal cells.

Benign and malignant tumours differ in rate of growth (slow or quick), capsule (present or absent), invasion (none or destructive), spread (none or around the body) and appearance of cells (fairly normal or abnormal).
They also differ in danger: a benign tumour is usually not life-threatening, while a malignant tumour is a cancer and can be life-threatening because it invades and spreads.
notes.tip: Past papers have asked what a tumour is and how benign and malignant tumours differ. A benign tumour is uncontrolled growth but is not cancer, so write the differences as paired points.

notes.b: A cancer becomes dangerous when it spreads beyond where it began. These are the steps from one mutated cell to tumours in other organs.
points: 1. A cell mutates and divides without control, producing a clone (a group of identical cells) of abnormal cells.
2. Further mutations and division form a small tumour in the tissue of origin, the primary tumour.
3. Angiogenesis (the growth of new blood vessels) supplies the tumour with blood, so it grows larger.
4. Cancer cells invade the surrounding tissue.
5. Some cells break away, enter blood vessels or lymph vessels, and are carried around the body.
6. They leave the vessels in another organ and divide there to form secondary tumours, called metastases.

Diagram: draw normal tissue (a neat single layer), then one mutated cell, a primary tumour with a vessel growing in, cells entering a vessel, a secondary tumour elsewhere. Labels: normal cells, cancer cell with large nucleus, primary tumour, blood vessel, invasion, metastasis, secondary tumour.
notes.tip: Expect to be asked how a cancer develops and spreads. Give the stages in order: mutation, uncontrolled division, primary tumour, blood supply, invasion, break away, secondary tumours.

notes.h: What metastasis means and how tumours harm the body
notes.b: Spread is what makes cancer so serious, and the harm tumours do comes from their size, position and appetite for nutrients.
points: Metastasis is the spread of cancer from the primary tumour to form secondary tumours elsewhere.
Secondary tumours contain the same type of cells as the primary tumour: breast cancer that spreads to the bones is still breast cancer cells, not bone cancer.
Metastasis makes cancer much harder to treat, because the cells are in many places, which is why early detection matters. There is more on this in Causes, prevention and treatment of cancer.
Tumours harm the body by pressing on and damaging organs, and by blocking tubes such as the airways, gut or blood vessels.
They also destroy normal tissue and stop it working, e.g. leukaemia cells crowd out normal blood-forming cells in the bone marrow, causing anaemia (too few red blood cells) and infections.
Tumours use up the body's nutrients, causing weight loss.
notes.tip: Secondary tumours are made of cells of the primary cancer type, so name the original cancer. Cancer is not contagious: it cannot be caught from another person.

keyTerms.definition: A group of diseases in which some body cells lose control of the rate and number of mitotic divisions and can invade and spread.
A normal gene that codes for proteins which stimulate the cell cycle; when mutated it becomes an oncogene.
A mutated proto-oncogene that is permanently switched on and keeps stimulating cell division.
A gene that codes for proteins which stop the cell cycle, repair damaged DNA or trigger apoptosis.
Programmed cell death, in which a damaged or unwanted cell breaks itself down in a controlled way.
The growth of new blood vessels into a tumour, supplying it with oxygen and nutrients.
An abnormal mass of cells that grows slowly, is enclosed in a capsule and does not invade or spread.
The spread of cancer cells from a primary tumour to form secondary tumours in other parts of the body.

questions.prompt: What is cancer? State two ways in which cancer cells differ from normal cells.
questions.model: Cancer is a group of diseases in which some body cells lose control of mitosis: they divide too often and too many times, and they can invade nearby tissues and spread. Two differences: normal cells divide only when signalled and stop at contact, whereas cancer cells divide continuously without signals and pile up into a mass; normal cells die by apoptosis when damaged, whereas cancer cells avoid apoptosis and many keep their telomeres long, so they can divide indefinitely.

questions.prompt: Outline how the loss of control of mitosis can lead to the development and spread of a cancer.
questions.model: In normal cells, proto-oncogenes stimulate division and tumour suppressor genes act as brakes, stopping the cycle at checkpoints, repairing DNA or triggering apoptosis. A mutation in a proto-oncogene can make it an oncogene that is permanently switched on. A mutation that inactivates a tumour suppressor gene removes the brakes, usually in both copies. Several such mutations must build up in one cell, often over many years. The mutated cell and its daughters divide without control and form a primary tumour. Angiogenesis supplies the tumour with blood, cancer cells invade the surrounding tissue, and some cells enter blood or lymph vessels, are carried around the body and form secondary tumours (metastases) in other organs. The secondary tumours contain the same type of cells as the primary tumour.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a benign and a malignant tumour.
questions.model: A benign tumour grows slowly, is enclosed in a capsule, does not invade surrounding tissue or spread, and its cells look fairly normal. A malignant tumour grows quickly, has no capsule, invades and destroys surrounding tissue, can spread to other parts of the body, and has abnormal cells. A malignant tumour is a cancer; a benign tumour is not.
